title: Java Dependencies and Supply-Chain Security
learning_outcomes: Explain the purpose of java dependencies and supply-chain security and identify when it is appropriate in a Java program.
Apply at least one of the lesson topics—dependency vulnerability scanning—in a small, readable example.
Identify one failure, compatibility, security, or resource-management concern and describe a safe response.

content.intro: In this lesson, you will study java dependencies and supply-chain security with a short explanation, an original visual map, a Java example, and a check you can perform yourself. Focus on the relationship between the rule and the behavior rather than memorizing isolated syntax.
content.why_it_matters: This concept matters because it helps you enforce security policy at trust boundaries and use vetted platform primitives. In this lesson, focus on dependency vulnerability scanning and use a minimal example to check what the rule actually guarantees.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: A reproducible build records its dependencies and build steps. Review direct and transitive versions, automate tests, and avoid embedding machine-specific paths or secrets in source control. The important habit is to make the assumptions explicit and use the code example as a small experiment.

content_blocks.title: How the pieces fit
content_blocks.text: Connect dependency vulnerability scanning with software updates before choosing an implementation. The example is a small, observable case; extend it by changing one input and checking a boundary, invalid value, or compatibility limit where relevant.

items.title: Dependency vulnerability scanning
items.text: A reproducible build records its dependencies and build steps. Review direct and transitive versions, automate tests, and avoid embedding machine-specific paths or secrets in source control.

items.title: Software updates
items.text: Use the standard library type that matches the data: java.time for dates and zones, BigDecimal for exact decimal arithmetic, and locale-aware APIs for user-facing text and numbers.

items.title: Artifact integrity
items.text: Primitive variables store values of the eight primitive types. Choose a type that represents the domain and range required; use exact decimal arithmetic for monetary values when appropriate.

items.title: Evaluating third-party libraries
items.text: Security depends on trust boundaries and explicit policy, not on a value’s Java type. Validate untrusted inputs, use standard cryptography and secure defaults, and keep secrets out of logs and source control. Apply that reasoning specifically to evaluating third-party libraries and confirm the result with the example or a targeted test.

content_blocks.run_instructions: Normalize and validate at a clear boundary, with explicit rules for accepted values. For ordinary Java SE examples, use JDK 25, save a complete class as Main.java, and run `javac Main.java` followed by `java Main`. CodeLeaf does not execute Java in the browser; use a local JDK for these examples. Preview-only and configuration-file examples have their own version or filename notes.
content_blocks.reset_steps: Restore the original example, remove any temporary output files it created, and rerun the baseline case. Do not leave credentials, generated private data, or large test files in the project directory.

content_blocks.title: Professional habit
content_blocks.text: Keep one clear hypothesis per experiment. Check the version, read the error message, test boundaries, and record what evidence supports your conclusion.

content.task: Try it yourself: apply the safe-coding principle in java dependencies and supply-chain security to synthetic data. Document the trust boundary, the expected rejection behavior, and the information that must never be logged.

common_mistakes.problem: Treating input or configuration as trusted just because it is typed as a Java String.
common_mistakes.why: Types describe representation; they do not prove that input meets the application policy.
common_mistakes.fix: Validate at trust boundaries, keep secrets out of logs, and reject invalid input explicitly.

common_mistakes.problem: Testing only a single happy path.
common_mistakes.why: Boundary values and failures often reveal assumptions hidden by the simplest example.
common_mistakes.fix: Add an empty, boundary, or invalid case and state the expected behavior before running it.

common_mistakes.why: It becomes difficult to identify the actual cause of a different result.
common_mistakes.fix: Change one factor at a time and keep a short record of observed behavior.
